en: Preface to the Direct Commentary on the "Verses on Ancient Cases" by the Solitary Elder:
There are four houses of the Chan school’s "Verses on Ancient Cases," namely Tian Tong, Xuedou, Touzi, and Danxia; these truly carry on the resonance of Fenyang.
As for the "ancient cases," they are the karmic conditions through which the ancient masters awakened to the mind. As for the "verses," they are meant to rouse and inspire.
The mind-mechanism causes it to flow forth. Therefore, its meanings may directly expound the facts, or cite analogies to illustrate the intent, or arouse delusion to trigger awakening;
taking the source of the mind as the foundation, using articulated sound as the rhythm, and making the accord with what is cultivated the essential point.

Yet, were it not for the revolving wheel of the mechanism, one would not be oblivious to what is manifest before one, nor could one give rise to the immediate object of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
It was composed thus. In the past, people compared Xuedou and Tiantong to You and Xia of the Confucian school; there must have been reason for them to be likened to those who praised the Sage.
Looking at the various ancient texts in the *Denglu* (Records of the Lamp), since these were circulated as one work with the *Sungben* (Text of Verses), they were valued for their verses.
This is because the spirited exaltations of the "host" and "guest" regarding the profound and the essential of that time were all expressed through verse. How could it be otherwise?

Examining and unraveling these works, one may glimpse the profound subtleties of the Chan path. Regarding those who have composed commentaries on the *Foshuo shoulengyan jing*, there are no fewer than dozens of schools beyond the two collections by Bǎishān Dànyǐn and Yuántōng Juéhǎi.
Those that are coarse and rustic approach the meaning too closely, while those that are fragmented and disjointed are remote from the intent.
As for venerable masters such as Fógù, Wànsōng, Línquán, and others, they gathered the essence of the scriptures and traditions, synthesizing the insights of various schools.

[The work] was long compiled and edited into a collection titled *The Commentaries and Songs of the Four Masters*. It assists in the flourishing of the four verses and briefly encompasses the subtle words of the five schools;

thus, the collections of Dayin, Juehai, and others cannot rival its legacy. Now, as the distance from antiquity increases further, the conditions for receiving the Way can no longer be entirely identical.
Moreover, what is called "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" (*songgu*) is already Chan that has wandered off the path, constrained by external conditions.
How wise! One must not rely on extraneous arguments but directly pierce the spiritual source.

Only then can the karmic conditions for the awakening of the ancient masters be stirred and set flowing, so that one may harmonize with the profound subtleties of the Chan Way in their boundless expanse.

This is the reason why this "Direct Commentary on Ancient Cases" by the Recluse was composed. Having retired to the mountain retreats, the Recluse sits before bright windows where incense smoke curls in green patterns, with nothing else to do.
Out of compassion for others, I have extracted the essential meaning of these ancient verses (*gū*) and songs (*sòng*) to thoroughly clear away all doubts.

In titling and concluding my work, I have spared myself the labor of elaborate rhetoric; thus, I have composed this commentary. When compared with other commentaries and song-interpretations (*píngchàng*), this truly surpasses them.

Nevertheless, it is still called a "commentary" (*zhù*). In reality, its nature is not that of a commentary; if it were treated as a commentary, it would be a subtle and wondrous exposition of the underlying principles, much like a sub-commentary (*shūzhù*).

This is not a small matter. Therefore, although I have provided annotations, I have still maintained directness; this is because I wish to be known for my straightforwardness. Yet, the underlying intent is not merely directness;

if it were merely directness, there would be no further depth to be found. This is similar to common worldly speech, which is not uncommon. Therefore, although I have maintained directness, I have still looked toward the ancients.

How much more so for those who clarify the reality of the Buddha’s teachings: they must have witnessed it with their own eyes and understood it in their own minds, rather than being entangled in the profusion of conventional phrases and verbose elaborations;

they must clearly realize the essence of the principle through personal realization of its active manifestation, rather than falling into the hidden lairs of subtle metaphysical abstractions; and they must truly comprehend the meaning of the words and sentences.
One must necessarily seize the opportune moment to manifest the matter, yet without falling into the error of clinging to substantial dharmas or to the person.

The function of manifest illumination must perfectly harmonize with the simultaneous [moment], yet without drowning in the partiality of emotional attachment or shifting positions. As for the distinct pointing out of the "eyes," it is like a solitary mirror suspended in space;
its latent penetration of the vital channels is like a golden needle passing through in secret. Examples such as these are not easily enumerated.
This work is the pivotal key to the Chan gate and a guiding compass for later students.

It is a pity that when this book appeared during the Zheng and Jia periods, it was so closely guarded within the monastic community that even its name went unheard. Now, more than a hundred years later, these long-lost pearls have been returned once more.

That the obscured light has shone forth once more is truly due to the power of Master Putong. Having realized the Samādhi of the Precious Mirror, he employed worldly wisdom to transform rubble into a jeweled monastery.
Furthermore, out of his compassion for protecting the Dharma and pitying the common people, he transmitted these verses and their commentary.
I was a fellow student of the Master and have long enjoyed our friendship; recently, he sent a letter to comfort me and requested my words.
By prefacing this work with these remarks, I have been able to provide a detailed account of the circumstances surrounding the solitary composition of this book.
Furthermore, I address all scholars of the Chan monasteries: The *Baoming Sanmei* (Treasure Mirror Samādhi) was transmitted from Dongshan and its radiance illuminates the five schools.

Do the scholars of the Chan monasteries today not wish to realize this Treasure Mirror? You must first apply yourselves to investigating the "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" (*songgu*) of the four masters. Is there [anyone who does not]?

In investigating the ancient verses (*songgu*), one must first apply oneself to the practice of the direct transmission (*zhizhu*) that is solitary and absolute. Through the direct transmission, the ancient verses become clear;
when the ancient verses are clarified, the Precious Mirror is realized. Only then does one not fail the teaching of the Chan Master.
I shall observe as the light of the mirror shines upon the monastic communities (*conglín*) without end.

In the summer of the Xinchao year of the Shunzhi era, the junior disciple Shou Dengpan of Taishan composed this "Direct Commentary on the Four Masters’ Verses on Ancient Cases" (Jingjue Zhizhu Sijia Songgu).

The Way itself has no difference; it is only because of the cultivation of it that distinctions arise. The universe is vast and humanity is numerous; yet minds differ and views are cluttered. Is this not so? Only one of great wisdom can transcend this.

"Virtuous One, how could evil be so capable of perfect penetration and universal salvation? It is because the former masters saw that students were mired in their mental faculties and obstructed by their environments;
thus, they exercised compassion and mobilized pity. By borrowing the host and borrowing the guest, and responding to questions as they arose, they set aside antiquity to conform to the present.
Pointing out the passages and the blockages, they composed verses and offered critical appraisals (*nien*). They brought forth wisdom to uproot folly—possessing substance yet devoid of form."

If one employs [function] alone, one will inevitably lose the solitary and precarious essence. To have function without essence is entirely hollow deception. To possess both essence and function is to fall into the realm of the ordinary and substantial.

To transcend both essence and function is to cling to the status of the honored and noble. To have achievement without rank is called "external succession. To have rank without achievement is called "internal succession.
To possess both achievement and rank is to reach both the orthodox and the deviant. When both achievement and rank are utterly transcended, one alone faces toward the ultimate illumination.

Above, strategies and expedients are applied with equal measure. Within the words there is resonance; principle and phenomena are practiced in tandem. Within each phrase, the spiritual capacity is revealed.
Using one capacity to seize another capacity, one strikes and robs within the very body. Using one authority to occupy another authority, one splits the arrowhead and seizes the nest.

Seeing attachment, one shatters attachment—this is called "seizing the emotion. Using a calculation to block a calculation—this is called "covering. What was exposed before is brushed away afterward; like a lion losing its tracks, the sage emerges from the mundane.

Transcendent! The phoenix soars to the clouds; words and thoughts reach their limit. This is called "absolute transcendence" (*juedai*). Adhering to the body without partiality is called "the pathless way.
Not falling into conceptual thought, one directly accepts it as it is. No "mysterious subtlety" is established; pointing directly within the light, the mind transcends all boundaries.

Picking up whatever comes to hand, there is no "this" or "that" among phenomena. With a single standard and an even mind, one realizes that objects are identical to the mind; returning along the very path, one arrives home.
The House: Absolute purity transcending all marks is the single color of great function; absolute purity with both [marks and function] severed is the single color of the primary position;

the seamless integration of principle and phenomenon is the single color of the present moment. When these three colors transcend [all limitations], it is first called the ancestral style of one's own house.

When these three colors adapt to circumstances, it is called "extending the hand into the marketplace. To linger in existence is for the mind not to forget; to linger in non-existence is to cling to emptiness and lose the essential meaning. One hundred...
All skillful means are collectively termed "expediency" (*upāya-kauśalya*). It shatters the chaotic attachments to differentiation and clarifies the fundamental source of reality.

When private desires are once expressed, public integrity naturally fades; when the Heavenly Principle is once clarified, the myriad deluded faculties naturally cease. Discarding the divergent currents of the ten thousand rivers, one travels alone upon the great ocean;
emerging from the greed and desire of the ten realms, one flies solitary through the high heavens. "Direct pointing" (*zhizhu*) refers to this direct indication.

The spiritual mechanism [of awakening] avoids falling into the layered strings of garlands of words. Those who respond to the occasion must directly grasp it at its core; only then will they reach the magnificent, fundamental wondrousness.

One will then know that this principle is neither cultivated nor realized, and how could it ever sink into the realm of mental activity? Having clearly understood this Way, one realizes that it is fundamentally complete and inherently manifest, transcending all stages and levels.
Without relying on effort or function, one spontaneously accords with it in clarity. I— (Note: The final character "余" (I) appears to be the signature of the author.)
Because I am so young and small, I have requested this with my knees pressed together in *huku* and offered it as a final instruction.

Should there be even a slight degree of understanding herein, I vow to carve it into print and circulate it widely, not violating my former pledge to remedy present deficiencies. I shall briefly offer these views of my narrow perspective as a temporary bridge for those whose path has been severed;
do not disdain these "herbal medicines," for they may slightly alleviate the ailments of chronic illness. I entreat you, Great Virtue and Great Benevolence, not to let this tradition be broken.
[The text] concludes. It is now being reprinted and reissued to reach future generations from afar. With palms joined as vast as the seas and mountains, I record this to repay my vows.
Written on an auspicious day of the first month of the Tai-cu [lunar] year during the Wushen year of the Hongzhi era by the śramaṇa Benrui of Longxing Temple in Hongdu.
*The Lone and Desolate Elder: A Direct Commentary on the Ancient Verses by Master Xuedou Xian,
Marveled at as Extraordinary.* Compiled by the Śramaṇa Daolin of Jintai Xinglong.
In the ancient Hangzhou Putong Chan Temple, Jingshen reprinted this work:
Emperor Wu of Liang asked the Great Master Bodhidharma, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? (He set aside both the conventional and the ultimate to ask directly about the Middle Way.)

[The Emperor] presented [the matter] for examination. Mozhao said, "Vast and empty, there is no sage" (so profound that not a single dharma exists; how can one establish the Noble Truths? One grasp and two cuts). The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me?

(failing to grasp the essential meaning; he pursues the words back and forth). Mozhao said, "I do not know" (a direct cut at the head; no room for confrontation). The Emperor did not attain realization (the provisional and the real did not meet).

He crossed the river and arrived in Wei. [The Emperor] asked Master Zhi (narrating the cause). Master Zhi said, "Does Your Majesty recognize this person? (the main intent is to seize the emotion; the meaning points clearly upward).
(To address the capacity of the student, he brings forth the provisional and the real simultaneously. The Emperor said, "I do not recognize [the true offering].

The Master said, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara transmitting the Buddha’s mind-seal" (pointing beyond the person to indicate the note; coating the inside with gloss). The Emperor regretted this and subsequently dispatched an envoy to retrieve him. The Master said, "Do not say that Your Majesty has sent an envoy to go and fetch me;
even if everyone in the entire kingdom went, I would still not return" (seeing that the intent was not grasped, he points out his outward flight).

○ (The main point is raised at the urgent moment; the meaning is clear, yet the blade is hidden within the phrase. Summary: (The two masters did not meet with one who understands; Emperor Wu missed the mark at every turn.)
The Noble Truths are vast and open (he brings up the previous koan). When shall they be discerned? (What is there to be discerned in this vast openness? "Who is it that faces me?

He replied, "I do not know" (since he missed the point, he could not help but be cut off). From this, he crossed the river in the dark; how could he avoid the thorns? (It was precisely because he failed to accord with the truth.)

Arms and weapons fill the world; the entire nation pursues them, yet they do not return. For ten thousand autumns and ten thousand springs, people can only remember them in vain (at the time their minds were coarse;

later, they regret it). Do not remember them; the pure wind encircles the earth—how could there be an end to it? (A single segment of pure wind pervades heaven and earth; who else could possess it? And yet, one regrets it.)
The Master looked around left and right and said, "Is there still an ancestral teacher here? (Xuedou saw people rushing outside; therefore, he pointed directly at the center.)

He said himself: "Holding the hook and the awl in hand, illumination and function are simultaneous. 'Call him here and let him wash the old monk’s feet'—seeing that he did not grasp the meaning, he was thus penalized by being pointed out.
A person such as this is fit only for washing feet."

Zhaozhou addressed the assembly, saying: (He casts his line for the sake of others. "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. (This is the fundamental allotment of every person; how could there be acceptance or rejection?
As soon as there are words, that is discrimination; that is clarity. (This causes people to set limits for themselves, seeking to distinguish what it is. This old monk does not abide within clarity.

"Do you all still cherish and protect [this] or not? (To be "clear and bright" is a great achievement; to "cherish and protect" is a form of discrimination. I do not even abide in the great achievement—tell me, do you still discriminate?

A monk said, "Since it does not reside within clarity and brightness, what is there to cherish and protect? (If one does not abide in the great achievement, how can there be discrimination? Changzhou said, "I also do not know.
(This means that since there is no path for thought, he manifests his "not knowing. The monk said, "Since the Master does not know, why did you say 'no'?"

While in a state of clarity (knowing only alertness and subtlety, yet unaware of the loss of vision), Zhaozhou said: "It is permissible to ask about matters; having prostrated, withdraw. (This is not a matter of words directed upward.)

One must not offend or oppose it. (The main theme is that he uses fishing as a metaphor for his conduct; the intent clarifies that great achievement is achieved without presiding over it. Summary: He does not fall into hierarchical gradations.

The Ultimate Way is not difficult (take up the case). Every word and every phrase is straightforward (the note says: there is no circuitousness). One contains many kinds (when released, the whole body manifests its function; "one" is "all").
Two are not of two sorts (when gathered, the whole function returns to the essence; "all" is "one"). The sun rises at the edge of heaven, the moon descends;

before the railing, the mountains are deep and the waters cold (fearing that one might stagnate in the two sides and give rise to false discrimination, he thus points directly to the state where there is no selection). When the consciousness of the skull is exhausted, what joy could stand? (Joy is consciousness)

If exhausted, there is no further discrimination; like a dragon’s roar from a withered tree, it vanishes before it has even dried. (If you harbor a consciousness of joy, you fall entirely into the Great Function—see the previous note on "raising the fallen").

Difficult, difficult! (Falling neither into the mundane nor the sagely, it is extremely hard to describe or appeal to). Discrimination is clear and bright; look for yourself! (Do not rely on others; you must fix your own eyes upon it).

Master Mazu was unwell. The head of the monastery asked, "How has your health been lately, Master? (This is a question of benevolence and righteousness. Mazu replied, "The Buddha of the Sun’s Face; the Buddha of the Moon’s Face.

(This is the heart of a parent toward their child. (Main idea: Directly clarifying the essence. The intent is clear and leaves no room for intellectual pathways. Summary: The question was posed according to human sentiment; the answer was given through direct pointing.

The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face—what things are these Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns? (If you understand the Buddha of the Sun’s Face and the Buddha of the Moon’s Face, then you will understand the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns.)

To cite one example [I ask you]: For twenty years I have undergone bitter toil. For your sake, how many times have I descended into the Azure Dragon’s Cave (Xuedou’s new interpretation likens the difficulty of his exertion to retrieving a pearl from a dragon’s lair;

it was only by exhausting all mental ingenuity that he reached this state). His hardships are worth recounting. O clear-eyed monks, do not treat this lightly (he speaks of his "hardships" for fear that those of high caliber might laugh at him in contempt;

yet fearing those who have not yet reached such a level, he says they are "worth recounting. At the end, he gathers both points together with two words, stating in total that one must not treat this lightly).
When Deshan arrived at Guishan, he tucked his outer robe under his arm and paced back and forth from east to west and west to east in the Dharma Hall.

Looking around, he said, "Non-existent, non-existent," and then went out. (He had come specifically to present his skillful means and test the various quarters, boasting that his insight was so lofty it was peerless.

The Master [Xuedou] added a comment: "He has been thoroughly exposed" (a single point right at the head; there is no need for further galloping). When Deshan reached the entrance, he said again, "One must not be careless," and then prepared himself.
With dignified bearing, he entered again for an audience (having already traveled to various regions, how could he act with such haste?).

While Guishan was seated, Deshan held up his sitting mat and said, "Venerable Master" (presenting a great function directly). Guishan reached for his whisk (it is in the planning that lies the victory, not in mere valor).

Deshan then let out a shout and, shaking his sleeves, departed (refusing to be caged; cutting off all incoming maneuvers). The Master added a comment: "He has been seen through" (nothing more than this; there is no need to...).

[This is] a display of self-conceit (a "one-point" or "two-finger" gesture). Deshan turned his back on the Dharma Hall, put on his sandals, and walked away (his intention was one of self-authorization; it did not exceed this principle).
When Guishan returned in the evening, he asked the Head Seat, "Where was that newcomer just now? (He asked with a double turn).

The Seat replied, "At that time, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall, put on his sandals, and left" (a truthful report). Guishan said, "In the future, this fellow will settle himself atop a solitary peak."

"The Hermitage Master scolds the Buddhas and reviles the Patriarchs—such is his solitary peril (that neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can tolerate him). The Master adds a comment: "Adding frost to snow" (he acts like this, and you speak of him like this).
(Main idea: presenting the pivot to examine the signs; the intent clarifies that the Great Function manifests before one. General Conclusion: (Master and guest mutually verify each other.)
First, he is thoroughly scrutinized. Second, he is scrutinized further, like adding frost to snow. He nearly fell (take up the previous remark; this reveals his hand and eye).
When the Flying Cavalry General enters the enemy’s court, how many can emerge completely unscathed? (He re-enters for an audience, like Li Guang who, having been trapped, was able to leap out.)
Rushing past in haste, not letting it go. Sitting amidst the grass on the summit of a solitary peak (even if one leaves no trace, this merely points to stillness and sinking into dead water).
"Alas! (Fearing that later generations might fall into a state of isolation and peril, he thus rebukes them, commanding that they must receive his instruction.
Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: 'The entire earth is gathered up and made as small as a grain of millet, then tossed before you.

You lacquer buckets do not understand (sentient and insentient beings are entirely without distinction; you have emptied yourself of all emotion, yet you still do not understand). Strike the drum for a general invitation to look (now I have specially gathered the multitude; everyone, apply your eyes). "

○ (The main intent is to use fishing as a metaphor for guiding people; the essential point clarifies that function is subsumed within the essence). Summary: (With a heart of urgent compassion). The ox-head is lost; the horse-head returns.
Within the mirror of Caoxi, all dust and grime are extinguished. (If you can understand the preceding line, then from Vulture Peak to Shaoshi, throughout past and present, it is all thus.)
All things are untainted. Strike the drum; look, yet you do not see. When the hundred flowers bloom with the arrival of spring, for whom do they open?
(Exhausting all your feelings, why do you not understand? Tell me, amidst these myriad distinctions, who ultimately is it?)
Master Yunmen offered this teaching: "Before the fifteenth day, I will not question you" (borrowing the light of the kalpa of emptiness, where questions and answers have already ceased).
"After the fifteenth day, bring me a single phrase" (since one abides in daily life, everything is as one pleases).

He spoke on their behalf: "Every day is a good day" (fearing it would become two separate parts, he again herds them together; here and there, leaving no seams or gaps). [The main intent is like casting a hook; the purpose is clear, yet the point is concealed. (A summary of his grandmotherly, urgent compassion.)

Set aside one; take up seven. Above, below, and in the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, there is no equal match (if you understand the first line, the four quarters and eight points will be seen as entirely non-dual).

Walking slowly, one tramples the sound of flowing water; looking out freely, one traces the tracks of flying birds. (If one can realize that dharmas are non-dual, they are naturally severed while in light and naturally revealed alone while in darkness.

The grass is lush and the smoke is dense; (with a single standard of equanimity, there is no "this" or "that. Flowers grow wild and scattered by the side of the cliff. (Fearing a fall into great achievement, an example is raised to break this attachment.
A mere snap of the fingers brings sorrow to the *śūnyatā* being. (Fearing a fall into non-action, another example is raised to break this attachment. Do not move.
"Touching it—thirty blows for touching it" (the current practice of the Dharma is not to commit these two faults).
A monk asked Fayan, "What is the Buddha? (seeking instruction). Fayan said, "You are Huichao" (a direct, head-on strike).
[The main intent is to strike at the point of urgency; when the principle is clear, he hits the rabbit in its den. (A summary: the tips of arrows meeting.)

The spring wind of the River Kingdom cannot blow it up (all the people of the land call out, yet they have never applied their minds). The partridge cries amidst the deep flowers (today’s request for instruction is but a single, ordinary lift).
When the three-tiered waves are high, the fish transforms into a dragon (Huichao’s place of awakening: transforming upon hearing the thunder).
Yet the deluded person still scoops water from the night pond (the ignorant person pursues words and gives rise to emotion, like scooping water at midnight to catch fish).
Cuiyan addressed the assembly, saying: "Throughout this summer, I have been speaking for you, my brothers.

Look—do Cuiyan’s eyebrows still remain? (Holding the probing pole in his hand. Baofu said: "The heart of a thief is always fearful" (striking the man on his own ground). Changqing said: "They have grown! (Biting the coarse with the fine.)
Yunmen said: "The Barrier" (a single dot, a single pick-up) ○ (The main theme is casting the hook; the intent clarifies the concealment of the point). Summary (The master’s song and response).
Cuiyan instructs his disciples; for a thousand ages there has been no equal (in his beautiful phrases, he does not reveal his sharp edge). Guanzi offers a response;

losing money and incurring punishment (he knows only how to cut others down, but not how to let himself go). The decrepit Baofu finds it difficult to suppress or exalt (his seizing and releasing, killing and enlivening, are naturally just right).

Cuiyan prattles on; clearly he is a thief (a blade is hidden within his words, secretly taking people's heads). Bai Gui is without flaw; who can distinguish the true from the false? (His words leave no trace.)

The sharp edges (of this matter) are indeed difficult to discern; Changqing’s intimate acquaintance with it means his eyebrows have grown (he alone permits those who understand the sound, skillfully grasping and skillfully pointing).

A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is Zhaozhou? (He borrows a matter to conceal his sharp edge. Zhaozhou said, "The east gate, the south gate, the west gate, the north gate" (using one device to dispel another).
(The main intent conceals the sharp edge; the meaning is clear and transcendent. Summary: (Seizing the trigger and taking the nest.)

Within a single phrase, the pivot of the occasion is presented head-on (a double barrier within the question; he yields not an inch at the outset). The Śakrāloka-eye is utterly free of even a speck of dust (the response follows the occasion;

both person and environment are simultaneously snatched away). The gates of east, south, west, and north face one another; infinite hammers and mallets strike, yet they cannot be opened. (Principle and phenomena are fused as one.)
The divine sword is difficult to distinguish).
Muzhou asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? (a probing staff). The monk then shouted (the great function personally presented).

Muzhou said, "I have been hit by your one shout" (giving oneself away while trapping the other). The monk shouted again (functioning but without illumination). Muzhou said, "After three or four shouts, what then? (no further response).

(“Is it so? Ha! Is it not so? Ha! After the shout, what then? The monk had no reply (he truly lost his illumination). Zhuzhou then struck him, saying, “This fellow who plunders empty air” (a great function that captures alive).
(The main intent is the mechanism of trapping the tiger; the purport clarifies the total presentation of the Great Function. General Conclusion: (The scale and balance are held in one’s own hand.)

Regarding the two shouts and the three shouts: the master must know the shifts of the occasion (if one only understands how to deliver a shout without knowing the shifts of the occasion, it is like "beating the grass to frighten the snake"—a forced act after the rules have been broken).

If one claims this is "riding on the tiger's head," both parties become blind men (if these shouts are treated merely as a means of capture and release, then neither guest nor host is clear; they are both blind). Who is the blind man?

Take this up and show it to the world! (Whether it be the guest who is blind, the host who is blind, or both guest and host simultaneously blind—if you can truly see through this, do not [remain] self-satisfied).
"Focus! You must verify this for yourself before you can attain it.
Huangbo addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you here are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine. Traveling as monks like this, how could you ever have a 'today' (of realization)?
[Being mired in names and stuck on forms, you are as if intoxicated by wine; practicing in this manner, when will you ever wake up? Do you realize that within the Great Tang Empire there is no Chan?"

The Master [Huineng] said, "What about it? (This is the simultaneous stripping away of both person and environment; the intent is to demand direct realization. The monk asked, "As for those in other quarters who guide disciples and lead assemblies—how do they do that?

(Since there is no Buddha-dharma, what is the use of opening the hall? Baizhang said, "I do not say there is no Chan; I simply say there is no teacher. (Since there is no teacher, all are merely fabrications. (The main theme is to search out shortcomings to reveal the long;
the purport is clearly to cast the hook for the sake of others. General Conclusion: (The scales and weights are held in one's own hand.)

A solitary wind, chilling and majestic, yet he does not boast of it. Dwelling upright within the world, he settles dragons and snakes (in his hand there is balance; how could this be forced effort?). The Emperor of Dazhong once lightly provoked him;
Three times he personally encountered the use of [the Master’s] claws and fangs (the Sage Ruler does not yield; how could he allow himself to be treated as a mere Chan guest?).
A monk asked Dongshan, "What is the Buddha? (Seeking instruction). Dongshan said, "Three pounds of flax" (plain and simple).

[The main intent is to pivot the head of the phrase; the meaning is clear and leaves no path for the intellect. Summary: The question refers to the time beyond kalpas; the answer refers to the present moment.

The golden crow is swift; the jade hare is fast. How could a skillful response ever involve a slight touch? (Dongshan and Xuedou act thoroughly for the sake of others. Displaying the matter to meet the opportunity, one meets Dongshan;

the lame tortoise and blind turtle enter an empty valley. (He simply says: "Investigate upon the matter. It is just like a lame tortoise and a blind turtle crashing into an empty valley—what year will they emerge?
Flowers cluster; brocade clusters. Bamboo from the south and wood from the north. (Ordinary reality is mutually pervasive; he provides an example.)

[Have them look. This brings to mind Great Officer Lu of Changqing, who understood that one should laugh and not weep (if you remain stuck in the affairs themselves, it is precisely the time to clap your hands and laugh loudly).
Aha! [This single laugh—is it a reward or a punishment? Is it an affair or a principle? I ask you to look with your eyes.]
A monk asked Baling, "What is the school of Deva? (He requested instruction from the master of discernment. Baling said, "Snow in a silver bowl" (Directly pointing to the center).
